II-H-01.note: C is the near-miss (uses the spoiled grain) but overreaches to 'abandoned'; only B pairs both halves of the passage.

II-H-03.note: B/C/D are all outside the passage's scope; only A tracks the final hedged sentence.

II-H-05.note: C is the best trap (arithmetic reversal) but contradicts 'daily pay rising'.

II-H-06.note: A states a mechanism the passage never offers; tempting but unsupported.

II-H-07.note: D supports only the 'made as working tools' half and is genuinely partially defensible. Also note A's internal tension: 'plainer batons show substantially heavier wear' cuts against 'seeing use only rarely' as a claim about the whole class, so the key is imperfect.

II-H-08.note: B supports the warming account; D is the near-miss but the passage already says thinning rates were similar north and south, so density alone decides nothing.

II-H-09.note: A is the strong trap: it shows breadth of borrowing within the register, i.e. exactly what the register already captures.

II-H-10.note: B is defensible: carrying stilted ants part-way reduces the overshoot in proportion to steps taken, the classic step-integration result. D is better because it isolates one named alternative, but D rules out ONLY optic flow, leaving the skeptics' gait and speed alternatives untouched while the stem says 'alternatives' plural.

II-H-11.note: Options alone decide it: for any authorship claim, a printer's account naming a named woman is documentary evidence and the other three are generalities. 'Widow' gives the gender away without reading the passage.

II-H-12.note: A, B and D all support the colleague, not the geologist; C is the only option pointing toward a volcanic source, so it is findable by elimination without weighing anything.

II-H-13.note: A, B and C are each factually false against the numbers, so the item reduces to a fact-check rather than a reasoning step.

II-H-14.note: 11.4x0.58=6.61 and 6.9x0.96=6.62. A and C are TRUE statements that do not establish equivalence, which is the correct hard-route distractor design.

II-H-15.note: B is true of sites 1 and 4 but supports the opposite conclusion; A and D are false (site 3 has 38 burrows and 9 cm; sites 2+3 = 20 of 50 cm).

II-H-16.note: C is false (B's range 1.4 vs A's 10), D is false (A's 11 > all of B's), B is false (1 > a tenth of 9).

II-H-17.note: A is true but shows the two running in parallel; D is false (74 is not double 66).

II-H-18.note: A is true but does not link slowing to retention; B and C are false against the figures.

II-H-19.note: D is the near-miss: it takes the same evidence one step too far by denying selection altogether.

II-H-20.note: A is the maximally hedged 'cannot be separated on this evidence' option; on a two-confound passage that shape is guessable without weighing the specifics.

II-H-21.note: C is the strongest trap and requires noticing that the 40-minute shift matches the real southward tidal lag plus the 'nothing indicates either scribe saw the other's table' clause.

II-H-22.note: A overreaches from 'confound present' to 'benefit entirely spurious'.

II-H-23.note: D is garbled rather than tempting; the item is really a two-option decision between A and B.

II-H-24.note: D is the near-miss but the passage says the reversal below 30 cm is independent of trunks and limbs, so excluding them would not save the figure.
